question: How do organizations and ways of organizing reproduce exclusion and inequality, and what would undo them?
Should organization theory say what organizations ought to do, and what warrants such claims?
How can scholars theorize what does not yet exist, or cannot be known, and still be rigorous?
How should a field settle what its key words and constructs mean, and does cumulative knowledge depend on settling them?
What do emotion and affect do in organizing that accounts built on discourse and cognition miss?
What can organizations do, and what do they owe, when democratic institutions are weak or under attack?
What makes a collective an organization, and where does organization end and other sociality begin?
Whose position, body and biography shape theory, and how should scholars account for their own place in it?
How do movements and collective action form, press on organizations and markets, and survive co-optation?
Under what conditions do new practices, forms and institutions emerge, take hold and displace old ones?
What are the indirect, hidden and delayed consequences of digitalization for institutions and for work?
Which neighbouring fields and vocabularies should organization theory open to, and how does it stay cumulative while doing so?
How should scholars work with practitioners and publics so that theory changes what they do?

What changes when a generative-AI system or algorithm takes part in organizing as a participant and not only as a tool?
How do digital media and platforms change how publics form, judge organizations and mobilize?
How is interdependent work held together when co-presence, formal roles and hierarchy no longer carry it?
When should organizations hold a contradiction open, choose a side, or refuse both, and how would anyone know the response was good?
What happens to expertise, the division of labour and workplace power when algorithms and generative AI take over tasks?
What holds a community together and bounds its membership, and what happens when it meets formal organization?
What makes an organization hold to its values or purpose under pressure, and how do its commitments change?
How do audiences come to judge an organization as legitimate, authentic or scandalous, and how do organizations answer?
What is an institutional logic: where are its boundaries, what variants does it have, and how do actors hold or change it?
How do people in organizations imagine what is not present, futures above all, and what does imagining do to organizing now?
How should organizing change under ecological crisis and other grand challenges whose shape is not settled?
How do stories, myths and narratives gain force in and around organizations?
What place should language models and computational methods have in scholars' own theorizing?

Can a person be an institution, and under what conditions?
Why do people consent to surveillance and data-driven control, and what would restore their autonomy?
What does it take to treat time, sequence and history as explanatory and not as background?
What part do non-human things — objects, spaces, atmospheres, ecologies, technologies — play in organizing, and how should theory give them that part?
How do local practices add up to macro structures, and how do macro conditions reach into local action?
Where does the individual stand — member, user, contributor, citizen — in organizational forms that do not contain them?
Do theories built in a few national, democratic, for-profit settings hold in other societies and sectors?
What changes when a technology stands between the people who organize?
Who answers for an outcome when no single actor is in charge of it?

How much can one actor do against the structures they sit in, and where do their resources come from?
When are resistance, dissent and disagreement productive, and when do they destroy?
When a new competence, practice or technology comes in, what happens to the old one?
